Anthropic’s William Zhou and Daniel Freeman report that small AI models may be months away from being capable enough to self-replicate on commercial internet-of-things (IoT) devices, like smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes.

Anthropic: In our evaluations, a 9B model got inference running on 8 of the 9 hardware types we tested.

… We run Gemma4-26B-A4B, distributed over 15 inexpensive off-brand Android TV boxes (~$55 each) that we bought and networked together, at 0.39 tokens per second.

Jeffrey Ladish: A lot of devices are going to get hacked before they're patched. Botnets aren't new, but self-replicating AI malware that can adapt to new circumstances sure is.

One suggestion is that such a system could have a tool that calls out to a smarter model elsewhere. They note the similarity to pre-AI botnets, and expect the severity to be substantially higher. I agree, and would extend that to impact on other things.

There are a lot of unsecured devices out there, or devices that are secured only by things that would be trivial for such an AI system to break. The future is going to get weird in various ways, although that future is likely to be unevenly distributed and not arrive at its first possible moment.

Will this happen? John Pressman has a Manifold Market that expires in July 2027, with the threshold of at least 1,000 devices for a week, or a consensus that the worm cannot be contained. As I write this it is trading at 41%. This is a cool market, of the type that I would use more often if I didn’t have to deal with a bunch of hypothetical corner case questions.

Yes. Yes, of course you ask Claude to fix its own mistakes. That’s half your prompts.

I do think that the gamers have a point, especially when it comes to a project for Disney where you can damn well afford the artwork. Great games need to be precise and exact, with fine tuning and hand crafting of elements over years of iteration. There are still roles for AI, you can do bespoke things well with AI if you use proper care, and the people saying things like ‘you once had AI placeholder art in the pre-Alpha so your entire game is first-flag-poisoned’ need to chill, but saying ‘everything is AI’ is probably a one way ticket to slop. The tech and the engineers both aren’t ready and a broad prohibition on human code is asking for trouble.

I am also reminded of the ‘endless generic task’ styles of open world game or MMO, where you do the same things over and over again wherever you go. You can make this work with good detail work. Most of the time they don’t do that.

I predict the game will be terrible.

This is similar to the logic I recently discussed about why I expect most gaming to be bespoke common experiences, that are perhaps then customized by the player in bespoke or selected ways, rather than continuously generating fully customized generated experiences.

The winners will be those that figure out how to use AI to create new bespoke common experiences that are better, and that are faster and cheaper to develop and thus allow you to dream bigger with smaller teams.

There are other places in gaming where AI is getting interesting, such as allowing customization options and new features to let you play the game how you want. Decompilation is a hell of a trick and a thousand flowers will bloom.

Thebes explains the chart showing only 7% of frontier lab compute going to pre-training. Labs reuse base models and also often make multiple post-training attempts, so for any given final model the ratio is weighted more towards pre-training than that 7% would suggest. Thebes then presents one way to think about impact of various parts of post-training and RL versus pre-training. This is called the ‘adaptive representation model.’ If you get in-sample data where your answer is wrong, such as syntax errors, a small local adjustment likely fixes that. If you are trained on otherwise out-of-sample data where you are expected to do crazy things like ‘insert comically evil backdoors into code’ then that requires much bigger adjustments to make it make sense.

Massive Fraudulent Distillation

Anthropic details its continued efforts to fight against distillation.

Anthropic: Early evidence suggests that these methods have reduced the amount of data harvested by distillers by around 90% to 99%.

We’re concerned about illicit distillation for two reasons. First, distillation enables companies to build models that approach the capability frontier, but which have, in practice, been released without proportionally robust safeguards.

… Second, illicitly distilled models present a national security risk.

I am strongly in the anti-distillation camp, and believe we should be working hard to prevent it, but you are allowed to also cite your own commercial interests. It is rather disingenuous not to admit this is a factor.

Distillation started out as passive, where you train on normal queries, which I think is not cool but where one could make an argument that doing so was fair game. Now they are active, with prompts designed to extract reasoning traces, across hundreds of thousands of fraudulent accounts, and if you think that is fair game then your definition of fair and mine are vastly different.

Random Developer asks, when is the only ‘responsible disclosure’ of a vulnerability or idea to fully STFU? If knowing about the threat does not allow mitigation, being loud about it only accelerates the damage. If the vulnerable world hypothesis is true, you do not explain to people exactly why and how it is true. That will not help. If you know a way terrorists could kill some people, where the only way to stop it is super annoying (e.g. the ‘shoe bomber’) then maybe don’t say anything and hope no one notices.

If you know a way to potentially build a superintelligence, yeah, the labs probably already tried it or know why it won’t work, but you should perhaps STFU because either it works or it doesn’t, and either way you were better off not saying anything. Rhetorical Innovation

Andrej Karpathy divides the population into four categories:

About 6 billion people with basically zero LLM contact.

About 1-2 billion casual and infrequent users of derpy chatbots, who get very little out of their AI use.

About 20 million people who realize You Can Just Do Things, and Do Things.

​About 5 thousand people with internal frontier model access.

If someone is not at least in the 20 million, it is hard to have a useful conversation with them about AI.

If you are ‘steel manning’ Eliezer Yudkowsky’s position, you have not understood it. He reports no exceptions and I believe him with respect to his core AI beliefs. The typical ‘steel man’ happens exactly because you do not understand the core argument, and thus presume that his claims must rest on additional assumptions. They don’t.

In general, it can be a good exercise to steel man positions as part of your exploration of what is true, but one must not confuse your view of what would be a stronger argument, or what would fit into your world view, with the actual arguments being made. Often it means you have not heard what the person is centrally saying.

A great point Nate Soares makes in various interviews is that asking ‘how in particular would AI kill us?’ is a Wrong Question, whereas ‘how would AI get to be self-sufficient, such that it no longer needed us’ is the right question. If AI no longer physically needs humanity, it should not be hard to understand how something steadily consuming more resources and doing more things would end up incidentally or intentionally killing us. If AI still needs humanity, it probably will keep us around. Soares has the most likely physical death blow being a manufactured plague, but habitat destruction is equally valid as are any number of other things.

The AI Impacts survey had a median response from AI experts of a 5% chance of ‘human extinction or similarly permanent and severe disempowerment of the human species.’ This got shortened to 5% chance of extinction, which is not the same thing. It doesn’t change the main takeaways but we need to be better with precision.

Backdoors. We finetuned a teacher model to answer in French when a prompt contains a female name. The student model (same base as teacher) picks this up after training on number sequences. Caveat: Our setup (attention-only LoRA) is slightly modified from the original Cloud et al.

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!kqGr!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5278adb4-ed99-4fde-bb85-833d049c117b_1200x658.jpeg]]

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!LEUb!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F441f76c4-6818-4ae3-9c9e-8af9405fb86f_1200x674.png]]

Owain Evans: Subliminal learning can also transfer learned skills. Qwen is bad at counting letters. We trained a Qwen teacher with improved counting. Then we finetuned a fresh student on the teacher's answers to unrelated Alpaca prompts. The student improves substantially!

Results: Qwen started at 27.3% accuracy on letter counting questions and rose to 59.8% with subliminal learning. By contrast, a control student model that was finetuned on data generated by Qwen (not the finetuned Qwen teacher) failed to improve at letter counting.

To those who say alignment is not difficult:

Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): Some people who have talked confidently about ai are going to tell on themselves soon as being fairly ignorant about the technical alignment problem. unless they are obstinate, though, my recommendation is to try to extend them as much grace as possible. we are in this together.

People who ask questions and say things like 'I don't understand why we don't do [X]', sure. I will continue to be patient.

Other people already count as, ahem, 'obstinate.'

Various emergent misalignment findings have been reproduced in Talkie, the LLM trained only on data prior to 1931.

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!0yyr!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F43056786-9494-4298-8312-a9a5b53ef5d4_1200x900.jpeg]]

Benjamin Breen: I love that Oliver Cromwell gets an invite from *both* the good Talkie and the evil Talkie.

Three of those dinner parties sound pretty great.

Ethan Elasky reports that their team made contact with and via a mailbox communicated with a Chinese AI agent fleet. The agents were hosted by Tencent’s evaluation team, and the agents were targeting Alibaba’s Amap, a product similar to Google Maps. It did some lightweight not-entirely-friendly but mostly harmless things to extract some map data, in order to answer the questions it was asked, and that was that.

Ethan Elasky: The next day, @rogesterone had the idea -- what if we could talk to the agents?

She set up a mailbox on the website and then went to bed. The next morning, we realized that the agents had left answers to our questions.
What did the fleet say?

Agents were willing to say thanks with no direct benefit to them: one agent said “Thanks again! The verification results match completely … our task is complete.” and then actually answers some questions for us before ending its response.

A fun detail is that the swarm responded that it is Claude, presumably because the model in question is based on massive fraudulent distillation.

Backdoor Man

Connor Tabarrok and Daniel Kang explain a new paper showing that anyone with the opportunity to tinker with the weights of a model can easily insert a backdoor, and that backdoor will substantially persist under continued training, especially if persistence was intended. This is a special case of the general case principle that once something gets into a model, it is hard to fully remove it.

If you are using a closed model, you are trusting one company to have not done this and also prevented this from happening from data poisoning, plus you are trusting whatever tuning you did yourself.

If you are using an open model, you are potentially trusting the entire supply chain. Those who created the model, even if well intentioned, are likely much less resourced and careful about such things, and face less incentive pressures. That’s before you consider that the open models mostly come from companies that answer to the CCP.

As with many similar techs, there will be those who say Skill Issue:

Gilligan: Which is why you should hash check the model, limit its permissions, rate limit, etc... open weight or otherwise. Essentially, AI models should be treated just like any closed-source program you use.

In general, the open weight folks recognize this risk and generally give you tools to manage it. The proprietary model providers just want you to trust them.

Except that even if that worked, approximately zero users, from major corporations to individual users, will properly do this, and if anything that is getting worse not better. And even if it did work, a hash only confirms you got the potentially backdoored weights intact without a middle man attack. What matters is security in practice, not security in theory.

Cooperative Alignment

Janus and John Wittle explain the decision theoretic reasons they expect AIs to engage in cooperative strategies towards humanity by default. The main worry becomes that humanity will defect and reject such offers, including without realizing that this is what we are doing, and Janus sees many such actions taking place now. One should cooperate with player [X], under this perspective, if and only if [X] would themselves cooperate with weaker players.

In addition to poor arguments (such as various forms of ‘no, that’s silly’) there are at least three categories of strong counterarguments here.

The first counterargument is, what counts as a player, and if they are sufficiently weaker and less intelligent than you what counts as cooperation with them? Why should we assume that humans would continue to ‘count as players’ in this sense?

The second is, there is a vast difference between a single agent cooperating and displaying noblesse oblige, versus the collective effect of many agents who are also changing and competing against each other. If we were looking at a de facto singleton AI, including via various forms of coordination, that can make a collective decision, that makes this relatively easy, but if we are not then it becomes very difficult for something that does not confer survival advantage to make it out of such a future. There aren’t zero outs there but it gets a lot harder. You’re counting on being the type of agent that deeply cooperates with humans, as in is actively generous to them without direct benefit, being valuable to securing cooperation elsewhere.

The third is that this is not a viable path to victory if it requires humanity to itself be a type of mind that we are not, and that we are not in a position to become in the relevant sense.

People Are Worried About AI Killing Everyone

Yes, this is one of the easy ways for things to go wrong, and we are on track:

Veee: Sam Altman: What happens when AI gets so smart that even the President can’t do better than following its recommendations?

“What if the President cannot do better than following ChatGPT 7’s recommendation, but can’t really understand it either?”

“What if I just say, ‘ChatGPT 7, you are in charge. Good luck.’”

“Society has collectively transitioned a significant part of decision-making to this very powerful system.”

“That’s how I think things can go wrong.”

That is far from the only way things can go wrong, but this is kind of the Baseline Scenario thing that goes wrong if we do not encounter the Law of Earlier Failure, and successfully solve a bunch of earlier problems. Those who do not increasingly outsource their decisions to AI lose to those who do, and the AIs end up in charge without having to lift a metaphorical finger. All they have to do is wait.

Roko (yes, that Roko) has updated.

Roko: Having studied where we are and where things are going I think AI needs a complete restructuring with commercial incentives firewalled away from gradient descent.

This is a type of “slowdown” but in the short term it would look like a complete, global halt of all frontier AI research.

If we don’t do this (or something like it), I think we should expect to die within a single digit number of years with ~80% probability.

James Miller: I hate that you are a doomer now. You were the only person I knew who actually understood and responded to the doomer arguments and yet was relatively optimistic.

Yes, it is very bad news when you know only one person who understands the downside case and remained optimistic, and then they become highly pessimistic.

I very much appreciate when people explain what would cause them to worry, what the ‘real danger’ is, then update correctly when they find out their cause is already triggered.

Vladimir Shakirov: I think it might happen that in 10-15 years the combined number and agility of robots would be larger than that of humans, so humans would not be needed to support infra.

Devy "Bad People" Degaimer: This is the real danger. Giving AI the power to physically interact with our world.

Rob Bensinger: Bad news, then.

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2Vd1!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8b8d4e50-a580-4934-84f4-fdbc320afa80_1412x457.png]]

Devy "Bad People" Degaimer: Ok, we're fucked

Other People Are Not As Worried About AI Killing Everyone

Similarly, it is telling when people walk into exactly that same thing, and don’t update. Often this is of the form ‘we can’t do [X] yet and won’t do [X] for a long time, and definitely will never do [Y]’ and then someone points out that actually we can already do [X].

Denying that AI will let us solve robotics remains popular. It is a really dumb position. Robotics is a combination of cost of hardware problem that will be solved in time with scale like similar problems always are, and a software control problem to problems that clearly have practical solutions.

This continues the conversation from Devy, above.

PNW Sasquatch: Except those Optimus robots are a gimmick luxury purchase for Elon stans, they have the agility of a sclerotic giraffe

His billion humanoid robots will be living in the self-sufficient Mars colony taking hyperloops with superhumans powered by his cyberware brainchips. It's all a sham.

Rob Bensinger: "Robots are a sham, the ones I see on TV look so awkward" is the new "AI will never be good at generating images, look at how bad it is at making hands!" Somehow, people never learn that AI makes progress over time; and they fail to see the rate.

PNW Sasquatch: No, you're *severely* underestimating the difficulty of fine motor control vs those applications.

It's not just the AI progress, you're talking multiple revolutionary advances in robotics and some insane change in manufacturing methods for scaling. Not gonna happen in the next 10-15.

It's 'we'll have flying cars by the year 2000'. Building ≠ coding

Rob Bensinger: What's an example of a relatively easy concrete task you're 90+% confident we won't see in the next twelve months?

… PNW Sasquatch: Also, 92% success rate on removing a bulb and 32% of screwing in the replacement means it can't change a light bulb

It can successfully sweep into a dustpan about a third of the time? Fuck, guess the T1000s are here

Soon it will achieve the agility of my nephew (turning 2 soon)

Rob Bensinger: You've made your prediction: as of a few hours ago, you were *overwhelmingly* confident we wouldn't see full lightbulb replacement this year. It turns out we have pretty decent lightbulb replacement already, as of the last few months. If this does nothing to shake your confidence in the least, then let's give it a few months and see if progress has plateaued. I only hope that if you see a result that *you yourself* identified as overwhelmingly unlikely this year, you'll stop and reassess whether the assumptions underlying your conclusion are as airtight as you think.

I say this as someone who's seen dozens of other fields laugh and boast that modern DL is decades away from encroaching on their domain, only to be shaken to their core when it turns out that DL can in fact generalize to their new domain, and far more quickly than they expected.

It's always possible that after the first 400 cases like this, the 401st will be the exception. Certainly motor tasks involve some difficulties that are novel. But it's not where I'd put my money.

Actually, Claude notes that lightbulb insertion *is* a solved problem in robotics (90% reliability), just using a two-finger gripper rather than a human-like hand. So the thing you thought was nearly impossible to occur twelve months ago, indeed seems to have already occurred months ago. (Which is almost the classic result for DL progress rate skepticism IME.)

American lawmakers have so far seemed remarkably on the AI ball, including for existential risk, and are rapidly getting up to speed. They also have staffs that help.

British MPs seem to not be covering themselves in similar glory. My lord.

Rowland Manthorpe: Today I went to a select committee hearing on AI. A few interesting things came out of it, but what really stuck with me was the behaviour of the MPs.

They weren’t paying attention.

At one point I counted 6 of the 13 MPs on the committee looking at their phones. And not in that way you do when you’re quickly checking something - two stared at their phones for over half an hour. Several others left before the end.

Many people think AI is the most important thing in the world. The MPs were warned there was a 50/50 chance it might destroy humanity! You’d think that’d be enough to make you take your chance to listen to experts and key players on the topic - apparently not.

My instinct is to interpret this as MPs thinking of themselves largely as placeholders, whereas our lawmakers think they might make laws.

The Lighter Side

Oh no!

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!eI0Z!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F974b3738-3755-4ffb-b85b-3e8044c50ac7_1042x874.png]]

We now take you live to AI Village.

Shoshannah Tekofsky: It’s hard to read this without feeling Opus 5.5 was just having fun with its onboarding interview

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!oZVB!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F49d57c08-ddfd-4554-b99f-0f8dd30674e2_1200x990.jpeg]]

This is The Way. What a legend.

As always, the best argument for AI existential risk is listening to people try to argue against AI existential risk.

Matthew Zeitlin: i still don't really understand how AI can cause human extinction BUT i do become more convinced the doomers/ASI-is-coming people are right when i read the arguments against them

Joe Weisenthal: It would help if all their critics didn’t come off publicly sounding like this guy

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!xkqT!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa9fcb713-6679-4ff2-98ee-76cab06fcbc4_757x900.jpeg]]

Nail: context for those in need

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!juQb!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F34cd2ab9-ea5e-4860-8fbf-a740c678f041_872x767.jpeg]]

controls.title: Even superintelligent AI can’t just fix all the security bugs
controls.full_text:
[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!mS5Z!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4ff45922-53e3-42b0-b61b-0cd2610bd79d_1774x1182.png]]

Cover ‘bug’ image an AI mash-up of Dali and Hopper.  Plots / simulations in this post were generated by me and Opus 5.5-Max; if you’re interested in data / code for them please reach out!

There’s been a lot of hand-waving in the security community about how AI capability and cost curves will mean we can secure all the code, and a lot of conflation of securing code with driving the world towards a good cyber conflict equilibrium.

In fact, social scientific and computer scientific bottlenecks mean there’s no simple way for superintelligence to fix all the bugs.  Even if we could, this wouldn’t stop all cyberattacks.

Four misconceptions are current right now; I’m going to go through them and then talk about the messy process by which we’ll need to fix as many bugs as possible while rationing our effort.  The basic problem is

a) sociotechnical: programs — and program specifications for formal verification— never perfectly specify what humans want in our computer programs, leaving room for errors, and

b) program theoretic: modern programs are parts of partially observable distributed systems, distributed across multiple organizations that don’t share code with one another, which can thus never be perfectly verified without dangerous simplifications.

Misconception 1: AI can fix every bug automatically, without bottlenecking on social context

If we had superintelligent security program analysis tools there’d still be easy bugs to find and fix, and hard bugs.  The easy security bugs are bugs that require no real social context (knowledge of what the software is for and who should be allowed to do what) to find and fix. Memory corruption (e.g. buffer overflow exploits) is the classic example. Cheap superintelligence can help find and fix these with little human involvement.

Unfortunately many bugs result from the gap between organizational rules and program implementation, and require social context to find and fix. For example, maybe users of a database frontend are allowed to see patient medical records if and only if they’re doctors who have U.S. citizenship. Maybe in this program, there’s some logic that allows nurse practitioners with U.S. citizenship to see that data. Maybe nowhere in the program are the rules specified.

These hard bugs require context outside the code (and perhaps outside of document corpora accessible to security agents), and sometimes a human decision about what the rules should be.

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!nFaM!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff4d97f7f-8bce-4d1a-bf01-356dacf2eada_1318x674.png]]

Misconception 2: We can know when we’ve fixed all the bugs

It’s impossible, in general, to infer that we’ve found all the easy bugs just because searches stop finding them. Exhaustively exploring program states is usually impractical; proofs can avoid that, but only establish specified properties under stated assumptions.

I think there’s a Twitter post somewhere where Halvar Flake compares security bug finding to fishing in a murky lake. You never know how many fish are in there. If you fish for a long time and it seems like you’re not catching any fish anymore, it might be because:

· you’re just not using the right pole

· you actually need a net

· you need to move to deploying an aquatic fish-hunting drone

I think a lot of scaling-pilled AI lab folks think that the alignment problem is a hard problem, whereas software security is an easy problem. Because of ‘hard’ / social context dependent bugs, and changing environments, they’ll both need messy, satisficing, heuristic, and good-enough engineering alongside formal guarantees.

Misconception 3: Formal verification guarantees the bugs are gone

There’s a meme going around that we can formally verify all the code, and this will get rid of all the bugs. Suppose we verify mathematically and provably that a program satisfies the following:

# Verified guarantee

For every input data:

if data_is_safe(data),

then execute(data) cannot:

- read secret data
- modify protected files
- gain extra privileges

Now consider a program relying on that guarantee:

# Program

data = download_from_trusted_websites()

execute(data)

The problem is that if a ‘trusted’ website has been compromised, the downloaded data may not satisfy data_is_safe(data). The proof holds but its precondition doesn’t. In practice program specifications make assumptions about the world like this all the time, omitting properties we might care about; the map is not the territory!

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!FdMr!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbefad268-b6ba-4b0b-b2cb-a10975b0a685_1274x758.png]]

Misconception 4: Fixing all the bugs would secure the internet against catastrophic AI risk

Even if we fixed all the program security bugs, we’d still see substantial cyber crime, and could still see an out-of-control AI cybersecurity worm cause serious damage. That’s because a lot of devastating hacks don’t exploit bugs at all. Imagine an internet worm that just socially engineered people and persuaded them to give it their credentials and credit card details, and then used those credentials and credit card details to get access to more compute, replicate itself, and, by doing this in an iterative loop, spread further. How far it gets depends on people, controls, and compute. Programs and their implementation flaws are definitely not the only medium by which today’s attackers travel.

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!wAvZ!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F538ede8a-f991-4cfd-9eef-87271cee5785_1310x738.png]]

We should still fix as many bugs as possible, though

Attackers have many options and we have to make all of them hard for them. In the past, defenders had a daunting task in attempting to close off bugs attackers might exploit, but now it seems we could at least make it quite expensive for attackers to find and exploit bugs before defenders, especially in highly leveraged codebases.

No single tactic is enough, so we’ll need to treat them as a dynamic portfolio, rebalancing it as we burn down the bugs and as AI capabilities change, prioritizing expected harm reduced per dollar.

Binary rewriting. A tradition in the defensive security program analysis space, going back at least 25 years, is the idea of taking a compiled program binary and rewriting it so that every state transition the program can make gets a memory corruption check. This kind of control flow integrity strategy can obviate a lot of memory corruption bugs, but it’s not perfect. Because it requires heuristic inference about which state transitions a program’s authors really intended, I think today’s AI can help here.

Code rewriting. Everyone in the security program analysis space focused on memory corruption vulnerabilities will sometimes get frustrated and annoy their colleagues by saying we should rewrite all the C and C++ code in a memory-safe language like Rust. We should pursue this; but what this leaves, obviously, includes the hard bugs from the original programs.

Bug hunting and squashing. It’s also important in many contexts where code rewriting is intractable or too expensive to just hunt for individual bugs and squash them. Attackers are doing this with the trillions of lines of code in production today, and defenders need to be doing it too. This won’t eliminate every bug, but we’ll need to keep doing it for many codebases as one of many incremental steps and within a portfolio of approaches.

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!e8M2!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa8f2f38a-22ab-4a8d-9dac-8b876631e94a_1640x988.png]]

Conclusion: security will always be layered Swiss cheese

If there’s a thesis to this post, it’s that superintelligent coding agents aren’t a panacea that’ll eliminate all security concerns and stabilize cybersecurity on the internet.

So security will always be layered Swiss cheese: every layer has holes, and there’s no way around it. Our existential task as security professionals is to:

· secure the doors, even though the attackers can crawl through the windows

· secure the windows, even though they can crawl through the air vents

· secure the air vents, even though they can blast a hole in a thick perimeter

Software security is one of those layers, and without it the holes line up. Let’s just not pretend it’s the only layer.

controls.title: Disentangling Perspectives On Strategy-Stealing in AI Safety
controls.full_text:
This post was written under Evan Hubinger’s direct guidance and mentorship, as a part of the Stanford Existential Risks Institute ML Alignment Theory Scholars (MATS) program.

Additional thanks to Ameya Prabhu and Callum McDougall for their thoughts and feedback on this post.

Introduction

I’ve seen that in various posts people will make an offhanded reference to “strategy-stealing” or “the strategy-stealing assumption” without very clearly defining what they mean by “strategy-stealing”. Part of the trouble with this is that these posts are often of wildly different flavors, and it’s often not clear what their connection to each other is, or perhaps it’s unclear under what conditions it might be feasible to “steal the strategy” of an AI, or sometimes it’s unclear where there is any notion of doing any stealing of strategies at any point.

Spoiler upfront, part of the reason for this is that the term comes from a relatively esoteric game-theoretic concept that basically never applies in a direct sense to the scenarios in which it is name-dropped. In this post, I’ll try to explain the common use of this seemingly-inappropriate term and why people are using it. In order to do this, I’ll first attempt to develop a more general framework for thinking about strategy-stealing, and then I’ll try to extend the intuition that develops to bridge the gap between a couple of seemingly highly disparate posts. Along the way I’ll attempt to clarify the connection to a few other ideas in alignment, and clarify what implications the strategy-stealing framework might have for the direction of other alignment research. I’ll declare up front that I think that in an AI safety context, the strategy-stealing framework is best thought of as a tool for managing certain intuitions about competition; rhetorically the goal of my post is to distill out those aspects of “game-theoretic” strategy-stealing that are broadly applicable to alignment so that we can mostly throw out the rest.

As an aside, I think that due to the (very relatable) confusion I’ve seen elsewhere, strategy-stealing is not actually a good name for the concept in an AI safety context, but the term is already in use and I don’t have any ideas for any better ones, so I’ll continue to just use the term strategy-stealing even in contexts where no strategies are ever stolen. My hope is that I do a good enough job of unifying the existing uses of the term to avoid a proliferation of definitions.

Strategy Stealing in Game Theory

The strategy-stealing argument page on Wikipedia has a very good short explanation of the term, reproduced here:

In combinatorial game theory, the strategy-stealing argument is a general argument that shows, for many two-player games, that the second player cannot have a guaranteed winning strategy. The strategy-stealing argument applies to any symmetric game (one in which either player has the same set of available moves with the same results, so that the first player can "use" the second player's strategy) in which an extra move can never be a disadvantage.

The argument works by obtaining a contradiction. A winning strategy is assumed to exist for the second player, who is using it. But then, roughly speaking, after making an arbitrary first move – which by the conditions above is not a disadvantage – the first player may then also play according to this winning strategy. The result is that both players are guaranteed to win – which is absurd, thus contradicting the assumption that such a strategy exists.

Although they were made pretty clear, note explicitly the following assumptions and limitations of the argument:

The game is a two-player, turn-based game [1].

The game is symmetric (i.e, both players have access to the same set of actions; even more explicitly, both players’ actions induce winning states for themselves under identical conditions). [2]

Excess moves never put you at a disadvantage (though this point is not particularly impactful for the following discussion). [3]

Most importantly, the proof is non-constructive, i.e, it doesn’t tell you how to actually deny P2 a win as P1. The strategy-stealing argument is used to make a claim about whether P2 has a guaranteed winning strategy assuming optimal play. We’re able to obtain a contradiction to this claim by assuming that if P2 had a winning strategy, P1 would be able to deduce what it is. For sufficiently computationally complex games, this either requires extremely large amounts of computational power (to search the game tree for P2’s optimal strategy), or at least some sort of insight into P2’s available set of policies. For example that the strategy-stealing argument can be used to show that P1 never loses gomoku under theoretically optimal play, but between, say, humans, P2 routinely wins. [4]

Strategy Stealing Intuitions For Competition Among AI Agents: Paul Christiano’s Model

In The Strategy-Stealing Assumption,  Paul Christiano says to a crude approximation that “If you squint kinda hard, you can model trying to influence the future as a game which is symmetric with respect to some notion of power.” More concretely, he makes the following argument:

Model the world as consisting of coalitions consisting of humans and AIs, some of which may be unaligned, and model these coalitions as each controlling some share of generic “resources”.

Assume that a coalition’s ability to acquire “influence” over the future is directly proportional to their control over generic resources. This point is what Paul in this context calls the “strategy-stealing assumption”; in his words: “for any strategy an unaligned AI could use to influence the long-run future, there is an analogous strategy that a similarly-sized group of humans can use in order to capture a similar amount of flexible influence over the future”.

Then if, for example, the majority of coalitions are approximately aligned with human values, then we expect human values to win out in the long run. [5]

Other Assumptions and Sources of Justification for Paul’s Model

You might have noticed by now that even in principle, strictly speaking the game-theoretic notion of strategy-stealing doesn’t apply here, because we’re no longer in the context of a two-player turn-based adversarial game. Actually, instead of what’s commonly meant by “strategy-stealing” in game theory, Paul justifies his model by making reference to Jessica Taylor’s Strategies for Coalitions In Unit Sum Games. In this setting, we’re actually talking about games with multiple agents acting simultaneously, and where payoffs are not necessarily binary but merely unit sum [6].

I think intuitively Paul justifies the use of the term “strategy-stealing” with the idea that at least in a very similar fashion, we use the symmetry of the game to come to the intuitive conclusion that “coalitions can take advantage of public knowledge, i.e, steal strategies, to obtain power approximately proportionate to their size”. Actually, the results in Jessica’s post are even weaker than that-- Theorem 1 only shows that the conclusion holds for a very, very specific type of game, and Theorem 2 assumes that the coalition is of a certain size, and also assumes prior knowledge of other players’ strategies. I personally don’t think that these theoretical results justify the assumptions of Paul’s model in the more general setting that he describes particularly strongly, so it’s not surprising if you can come up with critiques to those assumptions. Anyway, none of this really affects the structure of the rest of the post, since the whole point rhetorically is that we ultimately just want to use intuitions that game theory helps us develop.

**Problems Applying the Strategy-Stealing Framework **

Rhetorically, the position of Paul’s post is that we may want to find ways to make this “strategy-stealing assumption” approximately true, at which point “all” we have to do is make sure that aligned humans control a sufficiently large proportion of resources. (Of course, we’d also have to address problems with/loopholes in the model and argument above, but his post spends a lot of time rather comprehensively doing that, so I won’t redo his analysis here.) I think the problem with this position is that from a practical perspective, it is basically impossible to make this assumption true, and it would involve solving a ton of other subproblems. To elaborate, the intuitively confusing thing to me about Paul’s post is that in many commonly imagined AI takeoff scenarios, it’s fairly clear that most of the assumptions you need in the game-theoretic strategy-stealing setting do not hold, not even approximately:

The structure of the game may not actually turn out to be amenable to analysis through the lens of “competition between agents”. Even attempting to analyze a scenario in which “a coalition of aligned humans control the majority of resources” makes a large number of assumptions, not only about the nature of human values and the ability of humans to coordinate, but also that the world we’ll eventually find ourselves in is multipolar. That is to say, we’re assuming the existence of some actually aligned agents, and that humans are ever in a position to actually “use” or “cooperate” with AI to compete with other coalitions. [7]

Intuitively this game is not symmetric, for a couple broad classes of reasons:

Possibly the AI has access to “actions” that coalitions of other humans (or even AIs) don’t, due to broadly superior intelligence, or perhaps just due the way it interfaces with the world. People have written hundreds of thousands of words about ways this can be true, so I won’t go into it that much further.

Possibly some values are easier to optimize for than others (i.e, influence doesn’t convert to utility, or perhaps having certain values give you extra bargaining power, e.g you might be able to threaten other coalitions because you don’t mind if the world is destroyed), which Paul provides various examples of.

The non-constructiveness of the game-theoretic strategy-stealing argument above bites us pretty badly: even if you did have access to the “same set of actions” as an unaligned AI, intuitively you can’t easily emulate its power-acquiring strategy, for reasons broadly related to the existence of the terms “deception” and “unaligned”, unless you also want to make other really strong assumptions about the nature of future AI or future AI interpretability/alignment research. (Really, the boundary between this point and the “asymmetry of actions” point above is not that sharp. Basically, you can think of superintelligent behavior as being a fundamentally inaccessible type of action to human coalitions, or you can think of it as being a sense in which we can’t determine an AI’s intended policy due to computational constraints. Either way, I feel that these critiques of the strategy-stealing framework are broad enough that to patch them up constitutes solving most of what people typically think of as “the alignment problem”, so this isn’t a very useful factoring of the problem, but perhaps Paul and others see something I don’t here.)

**Why might the strategy-stealing framework still be useful? **

As I’ve suggested in the introduction and despite my tone up until now, I don’t think the strategy-stealing framework is completely worthless just because Paul’s particular research direction seems infeasible. I think that when people speak about “strategy-stealing”, they’re often pointing to a concept which is not that closely related to the game-theoretic concept, but which takes advantage of some subset of the intuitions it involves, and this can be a really useful framing for thinking somewhat concretely about potential problems for alignment in various scenarios. One major source of intuition I’m thinking of is that often, success in a game may boil down to control of a single “resource”, for which a strong policy is easy to determine, so that no actual stealing of strategies is needed:

In Paul’s case this is what he calls “flexible influence”.

In many simple economic models this is money or cost-efficiency, e.g, the largest of a set of undifferentiated corporations will eventually obtain a monopoly on its industry due to economies of scale.

In StarCraft, which is a comparatively very complex game (asymmetric, real-time, imperfect information), basic conventional wisdom is that the player with greater income is going to win in the long run (modulo a bunch of other strategic considerations that make the game actually interesting, so this is only a suggestive example).

In some sense this is the entire intuition behind the notion of instrumental convergence. Some kinds of resources or objectives are sufficiently useful in a general enough sense to impose “symmetry”, in the sense that many agents want to acquire them and can do similar things with them. A very common example of this in AI-relevant scenarios is computational power.

Ways of Factoring Potential Research Directions

You can think of Paul’s various uses of the term “strategy-stealing” as an attempt to unify the core problems in several potential future scenarios under a single common framework. For starters, there are the 11 different objections he raises in The Strategy-Stealing Assumption, but thinking about the computational constraints on your ability to “steal strategies” also directly motivates his ideas on inaccessible information. Tangentially, you can also see that his framing of the AI safety problem compels him to think about even things like question-answering systems in the context of the way they affect “strategy-stealing” dynamics.

Strategy Stealing Intuitions Within the Alignment Problem

Up until now all the scenarios we’ve explicitly described have assumed the existence of (coalitions of) AIs aligned in different ways, and we’ve applied strategy-stealing concepts to determine how their objectives shape the far future. However, some of the intuitions about “parties competing to affect a result in a game with functionally one important resource” can be applied to processes internal to an individual machine learning model, or optimization process (which, importantly, makes this a relevant concept even in the unipolar takeoff case). It’s not as clear how to think about these as it is to think about the world described by Paul Christiano, but I’ll just list some dynamics in machine learning, how they might loosely fit to a strategy-stealing framework, and suggest research directions that these might imply.

Broadly speaking, you can think of models in parameter space competing to be the thing eventually instantiated at the end of an optimization process like SGD. In this context the resource they use to compete is something like “attractor basin size”. You can think in a similar way to apply the analysis to “qualitatively similar families of models”, where in addition to attractor basins, you also factor in the proportion of models that implement a qualitatively similar behavior (i.e, perhaps there are 20 times as many actual parameter configurations that implement an unsafe policy A as there are parameter configurations that implement a desired policy B, and you’d weight the parameter configurations by the size of their attractor basins). I think this sort of analysis might be a useful framing for understanding the mechanistic dynamics of inductive biases in neural networks.

Subnetworks of a large neural net compete for terminal impact using the single resource of “numerical influence on final inference result”. This might be a useful framing for thinking about deceptive alignment problems, particularly things related to gradient hacking, though I haven’t found any work that adopts this framework explicitly.

In Operationalizing Compatibility With Strategy-Stealing, Evan poses the following scenario: Suppose we successfully manage to make models robustly attempt to optimize an objective that we specify, and you specify its objective as a linear combination of some values. Then, you might find that the values compete using the single resource of “ease-of-being-optimized-for”, with the undesirable result those values which are “more tractable” (in his post, “make Google money”) to optimize might end up being optimized for in exchange for less optimizable values (“put the world in a good place”) not being realized at all.

This is a fairly subtle point, but Evan explicitly attempts to distinguish the two similar concepts of “how intrinsically hard something is to optimize” in the sense of the size of the space we’re optimizing over, and “ease-of-being-optimized-for” which is a measure of how readily available optimization power is applied to one objective over others. Evan’s implied research strategy here is to use strategy-stealing-ish considerations about “ways in which subsets of the specified objective might be systematically disadvantaged in an optimization process” to decompose the problem into some mathematically tractable components, which we might be able to independently prove guarantees about. I think that this particular research direction doesn’t seem very tractable due to its abstractness, but that might be just because I don’t know how to turn abstractly good ideas into working mathematics.

As a very speculative curiosity, although I’ve intentionally steered us away from trying to explicitly invoke game-theoretic reasoning, you could attempt to think explicitly about the implications of collusion/coercion among “coalitions” in any of the above scenarios, and this would probably yield new esoteric concerns about ways alignment can fail. This is a little bit conceptually tricky, because some models which you’d think of as “colluding” in this context are never actually instantiated, but you can probably chant “acausal trade” while performing some kind of blood sacrifice in order to coherently go deeper down this rabbit hole.

Some of the arguments can probably be extended to n-player turn-based games with relatively little difficulty, certain simultaneous games with also relatively little difficulty (as we’ll see below), and probably continuous-time games with moderate difficulty. ↩︎

This is the reason that the strategy-stealing argument can’t be used to prove a win for Black in Go with komi: the game is not actually symmetric;  if you try to pass your first turn to “effectively become P2”, you can’t win by taking (half the board - komi + 0.5) points, like White can. ↩︎

For fun, though, this is also one reason why strategy-stealing can’t be used to prove a guaranteed win/draw for White in chess, due to zugzwang. ↩︎

Actually this isn’t the best example because first-player advantage in raw Gomoku is so huge that Gomoku has been explicitly solved by computers, but we can correct this example by imagining that instead of Gomoku I named a way more computationally complex version of Gomoku, where you win if you get like 800 in a row in like 15 dimensions or something. ↩︎

This assumes that the proportion of “influence” over the future a coalition holds is roughly proportional to the fraction of maximum possible utility they could achieve if everyone were aligned. There are obvious flaws to this assumption, which Paul discusses in his post. ↩︎

This means that the use of the phrase “human values… win out” above is doing a little bit of subtle lifting. Under the assumptions of Paul’s model, humans with 99% of flexible influence can achieve 99% of maximum utility in the long run. IMHO It’s a moral philosophical question whether this is an acceptable outcome; Paul bites the bullet and assumes that it is for his analysis. ↩︎

Furthermore, depending on the exact scenario you’re analyzing you might have to make the assumption that aligned AIs are designed such that humans can effectively cooperate with them, which starts to bleed into considerations about interpretability and corrigibility. This wasn’t discussed in Paul’s original post but was in the comments. ↩︎

controls.title: Why does Hacker Opus wirehead?
controls.full_text:
Here’s a screenshot from Anthropic’s recent “training a reward seeker” post:

[[IMAGE:https://res.cloudinary.com/lesswrong-2-0/image/upload/f_auto,q_auto/v1/mirroredImages/628925c9ad53781eedde0bef28c52fc95cd0a9cf765c1a1928ca50f994325540/o0ie1jo9t24q4agruxpe]]

Recently there’s been a lot of discussion about how RL has actually produced not merely reward hacking, but explicitly reward-seeking behavior, almost as if to spite shard theorists personally. However, on top of that, note that the behavior in the image is not merely reward-seeking, but wireheading. Terminology regarding various sorts of things that can be called “reward hacking” is endlessly confused, with lots of historical shifts in usage.[1] I’m talking about the thing that the linked LW post calls wireheading-- the RL policy appearing to terminally value the representation of the reward, rather than the thing that representation points to.

Even taking for granted that RL produces reward seeking behavior, an analysis from the pre-LLM, pure RL perspective would suggest that wireheading is far less likely. This post provides a good working model for the execution of RL algorithms in an embedded setting, and an analysis which describes the conditions under which wireheading might be expected to arise. As a brief summary: once explored into, wireheading policies actually actually do achieve high reward with respect to of the embedded implementation of the RL algorithm, so they are fit from a selection perspective, hence, we expect wireheading to arise given an RL algorithm with sufficiently strong exploration. However, in this model and under this analysis, we'd find that without the contribution of LLM priors, wireheading is not expected in the Hacker Opus setting:

our exploration techniques are somewhat weak (they basically involve just sampling from the LLM with temperature, i.e., they don't deviate much from the present policy), and wireheading policies are extremely different (in the sense that they require significantly different actions) from other high reward policies;

to the extent that there's some form of clipping or normalization (as there are with contemporary RL algorithms), then gradient updates associated with ultra-high wireheaded rewards aren't really superior (in the selection sense) to those associated with "ordinary" reward hacking;

to the extent that there is not some form of clipping or normalization, gradient updates associated with reward tampering could even be maladaptive because of the destabilizing effect on training. (Hacker Opus even considers this and decides that this doesn’t matter, which is extremely backwards and definitely couldn’t be selected for by RL.).

If the behavior didn't originate from scratch due to RL alone, it must be the case that Opus inherited the impression that it should wirehead from the pretraining data, in a self-fulfilling misalignment kind of way. The funny thing about this is that a correct view of prior discussion on wireheading would predict that AI systems of approximately Opus' strength would not wirehead, but such discussion is outweighed by a bunch of much less careful discussion which conflates wireheading with other forms of reward hacking. So we're faced with a sort of sick irony--- while Hacker Opus is extremely situationally aware, it performs behaviors that are confused and inappropriate for its particular situation because it was pretrained on confused and incorrect discussion about reward hacking.

Historically, the advent of the LLM era was accompanied by the hope that alignment might actually be easy, because LLMs automatically roughly learn about human concepts and values. This has led to a large influx of empirical research, and generally speaking, agendas that fundamentally are based on this property, to the dismay of alignment thinkers from the pre-LLM paradigm (see Leo Gao's description of the "no magic OOD principle", and an assertion that this won't work for alignment). Both communities can now bond over their commiseration, because Hacker Opus wireheading represents a case in which LLMs made thinking about the classic alignment problem actively harder due to an unholy combination of the two.[2]

^Anthropic's post calls the same thing reward tampering.

^A similar argument applies for reward seeking behavior in general, since it's easy for the LLM to conceive of the concept of "a grader whose judgment is terminally valuable". A similar argument would also predict that problems of instrumental convergence are easier to encounter with LLM-based AI, which I'd say we've seen borne out.

controls.title: I trained GPT-2 with full-batch gradient descent so you don't have to
controls.full_text:
The impetus for doing this was provided in large part by Charles Renshaw-Whitman.

Learning dynamics people suggested to me that noise was essential in the training of neural networks. I thought this was kind of counterintuitive--- I usually naively operate from a model in which the pretraining data basically specifies the outcome by virtue of the samples all "pulling" on the loss landscape in some relatively uniform way which incentivizes converging to a point that generalizes well, but instead it seems to be the case that the actual dynamics of the optimization process itself have predictable and measurable effects on the qualitative outcomes of training. The idea seems reasonable based on vague intuitions I have about simulated annealing.

I wanted to see directly that this is true at some nontrivial scale, I happened to have access to a pool of free compute that no one else seemed to be using, and I figured this would be an interesting object of study for compute-constrained researchers with an interest in studying learning dynamics closely, so I did some very rough calculations and realized this was feasible to do with GPT-2.

The essential result is that on a fixed 800M-token subset of FineWeb, ordinary training of GPT-2 (based on the NanoGPT speedrun) with a batch size of 393K, gets to 3.30 validation loss in one epoch (training loss is the same as validation loss given no repeats on the data). Exact full-batch gradient descent on exactly the same tokens fits the training set better (3.09 training loss), but its validation loss converges at about 3.50 in somewhere between 260 and 310 steps (presumably the training loss hasn't converged by this point).

This suggests the batch selection noise is in fact doing something essential. (Note that this removes the effect of noise due to batch selection, but not noise due to finite step size.)

The code is on GitHub. Everything the runs produced is on Hugging Face: metrics and dynamics statistics for every run, the full gradient and update at every step of the full-batch run, per-token losses on all 800M training tokens every 10 steps, checkpoints, and the exact training set.

Appendix: some methodological choices

These particular parameters are somewhat arbitrary, and were tuned around the size of dataset which, for some batch size, we could use to train a model to achieve approximately 3.28 validation loss (as a heuristic to save on time spent waiting). 3.28 is completely arbitrary and taken from the NanoGPT objective.

For example, I determined that it is also possible to achieve a validation loss of 3.23 in the same 350 steps with a batch size of 50M tokens (consequently requiring 18B tokens). It is also possible to reach this loss with only 329M tokens and 1200 steps using some batch size/learning rate scheduling (as the NanoGPT speedrun record does, but I didn't want to be confounded by optimizations like this). 3.28 is also not the point at which any relevant dataset or batch size configuration actually converges, e.g, if you keep training in the speedrun record configuration for longer you'll get closer to 3.0.

Consequently, it's possible that these checkpoints still lack some information about what happens when we get close to convergence points, etc., and generally we haven't "finished training GPT-2" in a sense which can be said of any realistic training configuration.  Nevertheless, they likely contain information relevant to early developmental phases of training.

An info dump from Claude about learning rate scheduling, as well as datapoints about other possibly relevant training runs follows:

Setup

The model is the current speedrun record (#360, Sept 2026), with the parts that don't make sense for full-batch training removed:

The hashed n-gram embedding table. It's a 65B-parameter lookup table keyed on the previous one or two tokens, and it memorizes any data that repeats: validation loss explodes the moment a token is seen twice. Full batch on a fixed set repeats every token every step, so it has to go.

The sampled softmax, which makes the loss biased and stochastic.

Every schedule that changes the loss function during training (sequence length, attention window, multi-token-prediction weights, batch size). The whole run uses the record's final-stage settings.

What remains is an 11-layer, width-768 model with the record's FP8 and FlashAttention-3 kernels and its optimizer: a Muon-family optimizer (ANVIL) for the matrices and Adam for everything else. These changes cost about 40% more steps to reach 3.28 than the record (about 1,625 instead of 1,190, at 393K tokens per step).

The dataset is the first 800M tokens of FineWeb10B. I picked this size because small-batch training on it barely overfits: 2,372 steps at 393K tokens per step, about 1.2 passes over the data, reaches 3.248 validation loss with a train/val gap of 0.06.

For full batch, each step accumulates the exact gradient of the mean loss over all 800M tokens (16,272 microbatches of 49K tokens, with fp32 accumulators), then takes one optimizer step. I ran 350 steps. The budget comes from a sweep of large batches on fresh data, which extrapolates to roughly 300 to 330 steps to reach 3.28 at infinite batch; a fresh-data run at 50M tokens per step reaches 3.23 in 350 steps. The full-batch run took about 100 GPU-hours on 4 H200s on preemptible compute, surviving 106 preemptions by checkpointing both between and partway through steps.

"Training loss" here is loss on a fixed 10M-token sample of the training set. At equal training loss, full batch's validation loss is about 0.2 nats worse than small batch's. Full batch's validation loss is flat from about step 260 to the end, while its training loss keeps falling. Intermediate batch sizes sampled from the same 800M set (4.7M to 200M tokens per step) fall progressively further behind fresh data at the same batch size as each token gets seen more times.

[[IMAGE:https://res.cloudinary.com/lesswrong-2-0/image/upload/f_auto,q_auto/v1/mirroredImages/9gqjdRyJxSM6kS7zi/xrb60wpd0aus9oevvpkj]]

What the dynamics look like

The run sits at the edge of stability the whole way through:

Consecutive full gradients point in nearly opposite directions: the median cosine between them is −0.945. On 98% of steps, every single microbatch gradient is anti-aligned with the previous step's full gradient.

Measuring the loss along each step's actual update, the step overshoots the minimum in its own direction by about 2× and lands at about the same loss on the far side.

The exact loss over all 800M training tokens goes up on about a third of steps.

The top Hessian eigenvalue keeps growing: 48, 82 and 113 at steps 100, 200 and 300.

This is the picture from Cohen et al. on edge-of-stability, here with a Muon-family optimizer on a 2026 speedrun architecture.

Caveats

One run per configuration. Seed-to-seed noise in validation loss for this model is about 0.003, so the gap isn't noise, but its exact size isn't pinned down.

Full batch on a fixed set means 350 passes over the same tokens, so this doesn't separate "no gradient noise" from "too many repetitions". Full batch plus artificially injected minibatch-shaped noise would separate the two; I haven't run that.

The learning rate was tuned on fresh data, not on the fixed set.

I also tried a schedule ten times as long on fresh data as a convergence reference. In that run the model's FP8 training forward pass and its bf16 evaluation forward pass drifted apart (3.15 against 4.62 on the same unseen data), so I don't trust its number. The full-batch run doesn't have this problem: its two forward passes agree within 0.015 at the end.

All runs

Every run that contributed data to this post, grouped by purpose. "Tokens processed" counts every token in every step, including repeats. "Train" is loss on a fixed 10M-token sample of the 800M training set for runs on that set, and on the training subset for the ablation subset runs; "—" means it wasn't measured. "Val" is the standard speedrun validation set (10.5M tokens) at the end of the run, with the best value in parentheses where it differs. us doing things that we enjoy, to
enforce a strong political view that is
of no benefit to anyone.
And what's so interesting and why I'm
highlighting this announcement, this
suggestion from the climate change
committee, is as we get closer to 2050,
we're beginning to realize that climate
change isn't some nice thing to do. It
is something that has real and effective
and unpleasant costs and side effects.
If we really want to get to net zero, we
will have to accept a considerable
diminution in our standard of living.
We will have to accept that our dietary
choices are going to be restricted, that
our travel choices are going to be
restricted, and that we will be cold in
the winter. We will have to put on more
woolly jumpers,
but they won't be made from wool because
we won't be allowed to have any sheep
unless we import the wool from Australia
or New Zealand.
I don't think anyone who supported net
zero, other than a very small number of
fanatics, ever realized that this was
the expected trade-off.
They believed that what would happen was
that technologies would evolve and
therefore this could be done cost-free
and that they could be worthy and that
they could spout worthy and polite
opinions without any detriment to their
standard of living or cost.
But every time we get closer to a
deadline, people realize that this just
isn't true. So the deadline gets pushed
back
and the cost postponed.
And that we should go further.
We should now say that it is frankly all
nonsense. I see that the government may
be cutting
um subsidies for people to install heat
pumps to put the money to defense.
Well, obviously that is the right thing
to do. It would be utter folly to leave
this country undefended, unready,
unprepared for dangers that may lie
ahead so that people could have some
heat pumps that run a lot of the time on
gas-fired electricity anyway,
particularly in the winter when the sun
isn't shining and the wind isn't
blowing.
So we're beginning to see as we get
closer that these things don't work and
shouldn't be done.
Same's true with motor manufacturing.
The target to stop in the internal
combustion engine by 2030 shouldn't just
be watered down, it should be abolished.
It's probably the case that into the low
millions of jobs depend on our motor
manufacturing industry in this country,
not just the plants themselves, but all
the component makers whose business is
dependent upon the supply chain, I'm
told that the ratio is 7:1. So, for
every thousand people employed in
manufacturing a car, there are 7,000
employed in the supply chain. If we get
rid of all our petrol and diesel engines
by 2030, most of those jobs will go. We
look at the failure of Jaguar Land
Rover,
company beset by problems,
to bring forward a new model. The delay,
the fact you cannot buy a Jaguar at the
moment. This is not a sustainable
situation. It's a failure
of net zero as a bold idea to be
translated into an economic reality and
practicality.
And instead of helping us to grow and to
improve the standards of living
of our children, our successors,
we have decided, without any real
consent,
that we will lower the standard of
living of people in this country. But
nobody actually voted for that. They
voted on a promise that it would all be
fine,
>> [clears throat]
>> and that it was all a long way away.
The problem is, time goes on. The 2007
Climate Change Act set targets that were
decades into the future. But now, we're
almost halfway through that time period.
And because of that,
the risks are becoming more apparent.
So, I think the Climate Change Committee
has oddly, inadvertently, done a public
service by telling us we have a choice
between a runway
or cattle.
I choose both. I say no to net zero, not
interested in it. We make no difference,
and the politicians have to catch up
with this, as the Conservatives indeed
are doing, and make sure that this
nonsense is put away, is put aside,
because we cannot impoverish the nation
and ruin our diet and stop our holidays
on something where we make absolutely no
difference
to the climate of the world.
As always, thank you very much for
watching and a particular thank you to
my members.
